title: Tri-Colour Marking Invariant
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Incremental tracing collectors colour objects white, grey, and black. The tri-colour invariant forbids a black object from pointing directly to a white object, ensuring all reachable objects are eventually discovered.
short: Maintain a grey frontier so tracing cannot lose a reachable object.
long: Maintain a grey frontier so tracing cannot lose a reachable object. Write barriers re-grey a source or shade a target when a black-to-white reference is created. The invariant is broken only momentarily inside barrier code.
proof: Any white object reachable from a root must be reached through a grey frontier; if a black-to-white edge appears, a barrier restores the invariant by greying one endpoint.
consequence: The invariant is the correctness foundation of concurrent and incremental collectors.

title: Stop-the-World versus Incremental Collection
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Stop-the-world collectors pause application threads while tracing, which is simple but can cause long pauses. Incremental and concurrent collectors interleave tracing with execution and use barriers to stay correct.
short: Shorter pauses are bought with more sophisticated coordination.
long: Shorter pauses are bought with more sophisticated coordination. Concurrent collectors must handle the heap graph changing during marking and usually stop briefly for final root rescanning.
proof: Pausing prevents mutation during tracing; allowing mutation requires barriers that record changes so the collector does not overlook newly reachable objects.
consequence: Pause-time goals drive the choice of collector design.

title: Write Barriers and Remembered Sets
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A generational collector records cross-generation references in a remembered set using write barriers on pointer updates. Minor collections then scan roots plus the remembered set instead of the whole heap.
short: Remember the old-to-young pointers so young collections stay cheap.
long: Remember the old-to-young pointers so young collections stay cheap. Card marking divides the old generation into cards and flags a card when a pointer inside it is updated. Remembered sets must be maintained even during concurrent phases.
proof: Old-to-young pointers are the only non-root way a young object can be reachable after a minor collection, so recording them at write time suffices to find all live young objects.
consequence: Write barriers are a small per-write cost that makes generational collection practical.

title: Conservative Garbage Collection
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A conservative collector scans memory without precise type information and treats any bit pattern that could be a pointer as a possible reference. It is safe without accurate pointer maps but may retain unreachable objects.
short: Better to keep a dead object than to reclaim a live one.
long: Better to keep a dead object than to reclaim a live one. Conservative collection works with languages such as C where pointer locations cannot always be identified. Interior pointers can force an entire object to be retained.
proof: Treating every plausible pointer as genuine can only retain extra objects, never reclaim a reachable one, so the collector is safe though imprecise.
consequence: Conservative collectors trade memory efficiency for language compatibility.

title: Bytecode Verification in the JVM
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: The JVM verifier checks that untrusted bytecode respects type and stack discipline before execution, preventing forged pointers and stack corruption. Verification is a static dataflow analysis over the instruction graph.
short: Prove type safety of bytecode before allowing it to run.
long: Prove type safety of bytecode before allowing it to run. Verification tracks operand-stack and local-variable types at every instruction and checks that all control-flow paths agree at merge points.
proof: Abstract interpretation of types along every control-flow path shows each instruction receives values of expected types, so malformed code is rejected before execution.
consequence: Verification is a key part of the JVM sandboxing model.

title: Garbage Collection Safepoints
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A safepoint is a program location where the runtime can stop all threads to inspect their roots safely. Precise collectors require threads to reach safepoints before tracing begins.
short: Stop threads only where their reference locations are known.
long: Stop threads only where their reference locations are known. The compiler emits safepoint polls at loop backedges and call sites. Stack maps describe which registers and stack slots contain references at each safepoint.
proof: At a safepoint the runtime knows exactly which locations hold references, giving a consistent root set; arbitrary stopping points would make root discovery unreliable.
consequence: Safepoint placement balances pause latency against poll overhead.

title: Unit Tests and Coverage Criteria
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Unit tests exercise individual program units in isolation. Coverage criteria such as statement, branch, and path coverage measure which parts of the code a test suite actually executes.
short: Coverage measures how much of the code a test suite has touched.
long: Coverage measures how much of the code a test suite has touched. Branch coverage is stronger than statement coverage, and path coverage is stronger still but rarely exhaustive. High coverage does not guarantee the absence of bugs.
proof: Instrumenting code records which statements or branches execute, and the ratio of executed items to total items defines the corresponding coverage metric.
consequence: Coverage gives an objective, if incomplete, measure of test-suite breadth.

title: Mutation Testing Measures Test Suite Strength
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Mutation testing creates small syntactic variants of a program and checks whether a test suite kills them by failing. A high mutation score indicates a suite sensitive to fault-like changes.
short: A test suite is strong if it notices deliberate small faults.
long: A test suite is strong if it notices deliberate small faults. Equivalent mutants produce the same behaviour as the original and are usually excluded. Mutation testing is computationally expensive because each mutant requires a full test run.
proof: Each mutant differs by one fault-like change; if no test distinguishes it from the original, that class of defect is undetected, so survival exposes a weakness.
consequence: Mutation scores often correlate better with defect detection than statement coverage.

title: Property-Based Testing with Generated Inputs
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Property-based testing generates many inputs and checks that a stated invariant holds for each. Shrinking reduces a failing input to a small, informative counterexample.
short: State universal properties and let the machine search for counterexamples.
long: State universal properties and let the machine search for counterexamples. Generators encode the input domain, and shrinking repeatedly simplifies a failing value while preserving the failure.
proof: Generated sampling explores many inputs beyond handwritten cases; stepwise shrinking removes parts of a failing input while the property still fails, yielding a minimal witness.
consequence: Property-based testing finds edge cases that example-based tests often miss.

title: Coverage-Guided Fuzzing
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Coverage-guided fuzzing mutates seed inputs, keeps mutants that reach new code coverage, and repeats, using coverage as a search heuristic.
short: Grow a corpus of inputs that explores more of the program.
long: Grow a corpus of inputs that explores more of the program. Instrumentation records edge coverage, and sanitizers detect memory-safety violations during execution.
proof: Retaining inputs that expand coverage focuses search on unexplored regions, and mutation explores variations of promising seeds.
consequence: Fuzzing has discovered large numbers of real security vulnerabilities.

title: Regression Testing and Test Oracles
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Regression testing reruns existing tests after changes to detect newly introduced defects. A test oracle determines whether an execution's outcome is correct.
short: Reuse past expectations to catch behavioural changes.
long: Reuse past expectations to catch behavioural changes. Oracles may be explicit expected values, reference implementations, or invariants. The oracle problem refers to cases where correctness is hard to specify.
proof: Storing expected outcomes from a trusted baseline allows later executions to be compared, so a behavioural change is detected as a regression.
consequence: Regression suites are the main defence against breaking working software.

title: Integration Testing versus System Testing
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Integration testing checks that modules interact correctly, while system testing checks the complete product against its specification. Integration tests target interfaces; system tests target end-to-end behaviour.
short: First check that pieces fit, then check the assembled product.
long: First check that pieces fit, then check the assembled product. Common integration strategies include bottom-up, top-down, and sandwich approaches using stubs and drivers.
proof: Combining modules exposes interface mismatches invisible to unit tests, while exercising the assembled system validates requirements that emerge only from the whole.
consequence: The two levels catch disjoint classes of defects.

title: Continuous Integration and Automated Builds
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Continuous integration merges changes frequently into a shared branch and automatically builds and tests each integration, detecting conflicts and regressions early.
short: Integrate often and let automation check every merge.
long: Integrate often and let automation check every merge. Fast feedback encourages small changes and makes failures easy to localise to a recent commit.
proof: Building and testing on every merge shortens the interval between introducing and detecting a defect, which reduces the cost of diagnosing it.
consequence: Continuous integration is a foundation of modern collaborative development.

title: Static versus Dynamic Type Checking
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Static type checking rejects ill-typed programs before execution, while dynamic checking detects type errors during execution. Static checking catches errors earlier but can reject safe programs that a dynamic language accepts.
short: Prove safety ahead of time or check it while running.
long: Prove safety ahead of time or check it while running. Gradual typing combines both by allowing typed and untyped code to interoperate with casts at boundaries.
proof: A static type system proves a property for all executions by construction, while dynamic checks inspect operations at run time and only report errors on paths actually taken.
consequence: The choice affects error detection timing, flexibility, and runtime overhead.

title: Hindley-Milner Type Inference
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Hindley–Milner type inference assigns principal types to expressions in a typed lambda calculus with let-polymorphism without annotations. Algorithm W computes the most general type scheme by unification.
short: Unification discovers the most general type automatically.
long: Unification discovers the most general type automatically. The principal type property means every other valid typing is an instance of the inferred one.
proof: Generating fresh type variables and unifying constraints from applications yields the most general unifier, which is the principal type scheme.
consequence: ML and Haskell families combine strong static typing with little annotation burden.

title: Exhaustiveness Checking for Algebraic Data Types
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Exhaustiveness checking verifies that a pattern match covers every constructor of an algebraic data type. A non-exhaustive match can fail at run time, so compilers warn or reject such code.
short: Ensure every possible value is handled by some pattern.
long: Ensure every possible value is handled by some pattern. Nested patterns and guards complicate coverage checking; some compilers use binary decision diagrams to decide exhaustiveness.
proof: Each pattern covers a subset of constructor combinations, and comparing their union with the full constructor set detects missing cases.
consequence: Exhaustiveness makes refactoring data types safer because missing cases are reported at compile time.

title: Weakest Precondition Calculus
subject: Software Engineering
statement: The weakest precondition of a program and a postcondition is the weakest assertion guaranteeing that postcondition after execution. It is computed backwards through assignments, sequences, and conditionals.
short: Work backwards from the desired postcondition to what must hold before.
long: Work backwards from the desired postcondition to what must hold before. For conditionals the weakest precondition is a conjunction guarded by the branch conditions; loops require loop invariants or least fixed points.
proof: Substituting e for x in Q is exactly the condition on the pre-state making Q true after the assignment; composition follows by backward propagation.
consequence: Weakest preconditions are the basis of deductive program verification tools.

title: Design by Contract
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Design by contract specifies preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants that cooperating components must satisfy. Violations identify which side of a module boundary broke the agreement.
short: Document the obligations and guarantees of every component.
long: Document the obligations and guarantees of every component. Eiffel integrates contracts into the language; other systems use annotations or assertion libraries.
proof: Checking preconditions at entry and postconditions and invariants at exit localises responsibility to caller or callee.
consequence: Contracts make module interfaces more precise and debugging more direct.

title: Software Refactoring Preserves Behaviour
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Refactoring restructures code without changing externally observable behaviour. Tests serve as a safety net verifying behaviour preservation across the transformation.
short: Change the structure, not the behaviour.
long: Change the structure, not the behaviour. Typical refactorings include extract method, rename variable, and replace conditional with polymorphism.
proof: Each refactoring is a behaviour-preserving transformation, and the test suite checks that observable outputs remain unchanged after applying it.
consequence: Refactoring keeps designs clean without introducing new functionality.

title: Coupling and Cohesion in Module Design
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities inside a module are, while coupling measures the strength of dependencies between modules. Good designs favour high cohesion and low coupling.
short: Keep related code together and dependencies few.
long: Keep related code together and dependencies few. Highly cohesive modules change for one reason; loosely coupled modules limit the propagation of changes across the system.
proof: A module with a single focused responsibility has fewer reasons to change, and weak dependencies reduce the number of other modules affected by a change.
consequence: These principles guide decomposition into maintainable components.

title: Semantic Versioning Rules
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Semantic versioning uses major.minor.patch numbers: a major increment signals incompatible API changes, a minor increment adds backward-compatible functionality, and a patch increment makes backward-compatible fixes.
short: Version numbers encode the compatibility impact of a release.
long: Version numbers encode the compatibility impact of a release. Pre-release identifiers and build metadata extend the basic format. Consumers can express dependency constraints using these rules.
proof: The specification defines each component's meaning, so comparing two versions determines whether an upgrade should preserve existing clients.
consequence: Semantic versioning makes dependency management predictable.

title: Technical Debt Metaphor
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Technical debt describes the future maintenance cost of choosing a quick, limited solution over a more robust one. Like financial debt it accumulates interest when deferred work makes later changes harder.
short: A quick fix today can make every future change more expensive.
long: A quick fix today can make every future change more expensive. Debt may be deliberate and beneficial when a short-term goal justifies it, but it becomes harmful when it is invisible or never repaid.
proof: A shortcut leaves code harder to understand or extend, so subsequent changes require more effort than they would in a clean design.
consequence: Making debt visible helps teams schedule remediation.

title: Cyclomatic Complexity of Control Flow
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Cyclomatic complexity of a control-flow graph is E minus N plus twice the number of connected components. It bounds the number of linearly independent execution paths and is used as a code complexity metric.
short: Count independent paths as a measure of testing difficulty.
long: Count independent paths as a measure of testing difficulty. For a single connected component the formula reduces to E minus N plus two. High cyclomatic complexity correlates with harder-to-test code.
proof: The cyclomatic number of a graph counts independent cycles, which for a single-entry single-exit flow graph equals the maximum number of independent execution paths.
consequence: The metric is widely used to flag functions that need more testing or refactoring.

title: Needham-Schroeder Protocol and Replay
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The original Needham–Schroeder symmetric-key protocol is vulnerable to replay: if an old session key is recovered, an attacker can replay a recorded message and convince a principal to accept that key.
short: A valid old message can be reused when freshness is not tied to a new nonce.
long: A valid old message can be reused when freshness is not tied to a new nonce. The Lowe attack on the public-key variant similarly exploits a missing identity check in the response message.
proof: The replayed message carries no nonce freshly generated by the receiving principal in the current run, so it is accepted as evidence of a new session key.
consequence: The attack established that freshness mechanisms are indispensable in authentication protocols.

title: Kerberos Ticket-Based Authentication
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Kerberos authenticates clients to services using tickets issued by a trusted key distribution centre. A ticket contains a session key and client identity encrypted for the service, so the client never sends its password.
short: A trusted third party issues encrypted tickets that prove identity.
long: A trusted third party issues encrypted tickets that prove identity. The ticket-granting ticket lets a client obtain service tickets without re-entering its password; authenticators with timestamps prevent replay.
proof: Only the intended service can decrypt its ticket, and the client proves knowledge of the enclosed session key with a fresh authenticator, giving mutual authentication.
consequence: Kerberos underpins single sign-on in many enterprise environments.
